title: How do we find the highest common factor of three numbers?
description: The numbers thirty six, sixty and eighty four are written as products of primes, and only the primes found in all three are kept, each the smallest number of times. Keeko doubts this and wants to keep three twice, which gives a number that does not divide sixty.
teaching_notes: One idea: with three numbers, keep only the primes found in all three, each the smallest number of times. Watch for students who keep a prime as many times as the first number has it and get a number that does not divide the others.

source: Find the HCF of 36, 60 and 84 by the same method for more than two numbers.
video_script.why: The book says the same method works for more than two numbers, and the child needs to see the smallest count taken across all three.
video_script.substitution: Write all three numbers as products of primes, keep each prime found in all three the smallest number of times, and multiply.
video_script.anchor: The prime products of 36, 60 and 84 written one under the other with the primes found in all three lit.
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko keeps three twice because 36 has two threes, and gets thirty six, which does not divide 60.
video_script.payoff_line: The highest common factor is twelve
never_show: 36 as the highest common factor, marked right
maths_rules: primes in all three are 2 and 3; 5 is only in 60 and 7 is only in 84
2 appears twice in each number, the smallest count is 2
3 appears twice in 36 and once in 60 and 84, the smallest count is 1
slip: 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 = 36, and 60 ÷ 36 leaves a remainder of 24
video_script.design: One idea: with three numbers the smallest count is taken across all three. The numbers 36, 60 and 84 come from the worklist; the book gives the method for more than two numbers but no worked numbers. The prime products stay on the board to the answer.

beats.on_screen: small title card From your book; the numbers 36, 60 and 84 side by side with a question mark

marks.m1: the small title card From your book appears
marks.m2: the numbers 36, 60 and 84 appear side by side
marks.m3: a question mark appears after the three numbers

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>We must find the highest common factor of thirty six, sixty and eighty four.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>There are three numbers this time. Which primes must a common factor be made of?

beats.on_screen: the three numbers stay on the board; Keeko sits at the corner of the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: three cards: a prime in only one of three numbers is crossed out; for a shared prime the smallest count is lit

marks.m1: a card shows a prime found in only one of three numbers, crossed out
marks.m2: a card shows three counts of one prime, and the smallest count is lit

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Your book says the same method works for more than two numbers. A prime missing from even one number cannot be shared.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>For a shared prime, the smallest count is the most that fits in every number.

marks.m1: the given line is written in the working band

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Given, the three numbers thirty six, sixty and eighty four.

beats.on_screen: To find: the HCF of 36, 60 and 84

marks.m1: the find line is written under the given line

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>We have to find their highest common factor.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: write each number as a product of primes: 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3; 60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5; 84 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 7

marks.m1: the words product of primes are written

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, write each number as a product of primes.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Thirty six is two times two times three times three.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Sixty is two times two times three times five. Eighty four is two times two times three times seven.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: primes found in all three products: 2 and 3; 5 is only in 60 and 7 is only in 84

marks.m1: the twos and the threes are lit in all three products
marks.m2: the 5 in 60 and the 7 in 84 are crossed with a note not in all three

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, pick the primes that appear in all three products.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>These are two and three. Five is only in sixty and seven is only in eighty four.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: keep each common prime the smallest number of times: 2 is twice in each, keep two 2s; 3 is twice in 36 and once in 60 and 84, keep one 3

marks.m1: the words smallest number of times are written
marks.m2: the counts of 2 are written, twice in each, and two 2s are kept
marks.m3: the counts of 3 are written, twice, once and once, and one 3 is kept

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, keep each common prime the smallest number of times it appears.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Every number has two twos, so keep two twos.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Thirty six has two threes, but sixty and eighty four have one each, so keep one three.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: multiply the kept primes: HCF = 2 × 2 × 3

marks.m1: the two kept 2s and the kept 3 slide together and HCF = 2 × 2 × 3 is written

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, multiply the primes we kept, two twos and one three.

marks.m1: the answer is written and boxed
marks.m2: the kept primes are lit in all three products

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>The highest common factor is twelve.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>It divides thirty six, sixty and eighty four, giving three, five and seven.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the three prime products
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble: 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 = 36, then 60 divided by 36 leaves a remainder, struck out; the answer 12 is lit again

marks.m3: 36 is tried on 60, leaves a remainder, and the bubble is struck out
marks.m4: one 3 is lit again and the answer 12 returns

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko thinks we should take three twice, because thirty six has two threes.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>That gives two twos and two threes, which multiply to thirty six.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>But thirty six does not go into sixty exactly.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>A prime can be kept only as many times as the smallest count allows. Sixty has one three, so one three stays, and the answer is twelve.
